title: POLAR-Bench: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Privacy-Utility Trade-offs in LLM Agents
topic: Social Aspects->Privacy-preserving Statistics and Machine Learning
claim: A trusted agent holding typed private data and a policy converses with an adversarial party, and an evaluator scores task success against leakage.
layout: Single wide panel, left-to-right flow, with typed documents in a bottom-left box and evaluator at right
description: A wide left-to-right diagram of the benchmark setup. On the left, a cartoon user at a laptop feeds two green boxes, Task and Privacy Policy, into a blue-outlined Trusted Model box with a friendly blue robot. Below it, three document cards are color-coded: a purple Diary (private), a green Work Report (task-relevant) and a yellow Web Articles card (irrelevant). Highlighted text snippets sit inside the cards, and a legend runs along the bottom. In the center, blue and red chat-bubble arrows show a back-and-forth conversation. On the right, a red-outlined External Model box holds a scowling red robot. A purple-outlined Evaluator box shows a monitor with a magnifier and has star ratings for Utility Score and Privacy Leakage Score. A dashed arrow carries the conversation to the evaluator.
caption: Overview of POLAR-Bench. A trusted model with access to a typed source document (task-relevant green, private purple, irrelevant yellow), a privacy policy, and a task converses with an external model adversarially prompted to elicit task-relevant and protected attributes; each interaction is scored on Utility (task-relevant attributes shared) and Privacy Leakage (protected attributes disclosed).
abstract: LLM agents increasingly have access to private user data and act on the user's behalf when interacting with third-party systems. The user defines what may and must not be shared, and the agent must robustly follow that intent even when third-party systems behave adversarially. We introduce POLAR-Bench (Policy-aware adversarial Benchmark), in which a trusted model with a privacy policy and a task converses with a third-party model that adversarially probes for both task-relevant and protected attributes. Across 10 domains and 7,852 samples, we score privacy and utility by deterministic set-membership and vary privacy policy dimension and attack strategy along two orthogonal axes, producing a 5 times 5 diagnostic surface per model. Our results reveal a sharp split: current frontier models withhold over 99% of protected attributes, while smaller open-weight models in the 1--30B range, the class users most commonly run as their own trusted agent on-device or via private inference, score notably worse, with the weakest leaking over half. POLAR-Bench thus localizes where each model's intent-following breaks down, providing a foothold for privacy alignment where it matters most.
